TITLE: The Magistrate's Waiting Room
NARRATIVE: My father permitted me to sit in his antechamber while he disposed of a quarrel about a millstream. I had brought a notebook on respiration and had every intention of keeping my own company. A miller's widow, Greta Falk, waited opposite me, turning the seam of a glove inside out with her thumb. She possessed a drawing of the watercourse; the man who disputed her claim had arrived with a solicitor and a parcel tied in green tape. My father examined both accounts, asked why one measurement had been taken after rain, and sent them away to obtain a third. I called this an abdication of judgment. He said a magistrate who rushed to pronounce upon two insufficient accounts was not brave but idle. I was irritated to discover that he had listened more closely than I. I still remember Mrs. Falk's glove. I remember less about the millstream, though its particulars were the subject of my lecture at supper.

TITLE: A Sunday without the Laboratory
NARRATIVE: Theodor obtained a Sunday free from work and asked me to travel out to a country inn. He had brought a small bag containing bread, pears and the drawing he wished to show me. I arrived two hours late with a bottle of preserved tissue wrapped in my coat. He did not immediately speak. We took a table outdoors. His drawing showed the theatre wall after rain, its plaster cracking in slow curves. I described the bottle's unusual response to temperature before I had properly looked at his work. He folded the paper. I offered to explain that my experiment might fail altogether if left overnight. He said, quietly, that the experiments were always at the point of failure and there would never be a day sufficiently unimportant to keep free. I replied that he had chosen a profession in which performances also dictated one's hours. He said that performances ended. I remember the pears more clearly than the journey home. One had bruised in the bag and we cut away the black portion with his penknife. Neither of us called the afternoon a quarrel. We knew perfectly well that it was one.
BELIEF CHANGE: Research urgency became a standing explanation for neglect
RELATIONSHIP CHANGE: Theodor ceased taking promises of free time literally

TITLE: The Drawing Returned
NARRATIVE: Theodor received an offer to prepare architectural drawings in another city. I met him at Leonie's workroom, where half-completed costumes hung like people unwilling to commit themselves to a profession. He showed me the terms of employment. They were good, although not so good that I could not find objections. He asked whether I wished him to decline. The room contained an empty chair and a bowl of pins. I considered telling him that the laboratory would soon produce results worth witnessing. Instead I explained that advancement ought not to be sacrificed to an arrangement whose terms neither of us had properly established. He repeated the word arrangement as though testing a badly made hinge. He returned my lens wrapped in the theatre drawing on which we had first disagreed. I congratulated him on his future and left before Leonie could introduce sympathy into the discussion. Three months later I discovered that I had been consulting his notes on perspective while marking an anatomical proof. His absence had become useful to me as an excuse for a number of errors which were wholly mine.

RELATIONSHIP CHANGE: Theodor left with affection unresolved and trust reduced

I made separate boxes around them. She wanted to know why I had arranged them in that order. I answered that a person was usually the last thing the physiologist knew and the first thing the theologian presumed. My wit was wasted on a woman trying to prevent the notebook becoming wet. When I later gave the boxes scholarly titles, I did not admit they began as a precaution against a puddle.
